title: CLI and developer tools
covers: Command-line tools, scripts, installers, SDKs, plugins and other tools a developer or owner runs.

stakeholders.who: Someone installing and running the tool for the first time, often on another machine
cares_about: it installs and runs the first time
error messages that say how to fix it
would_notice: a stack trace instead of a message
--help that lists flags without saying what they do
it only works on the author's machine or without spaces in the path

stakeholders.who: Someone using the tool in a script, a pipe or CI
would_notice: progress text mixed into the JSON output
a hang waiting for input in CI

stakeholders.who: The person who releases and updates the tool
cares_about: tests that cover the command-line contract
a release users can actually see
would_notice: no test for exit codes or stderr
a version number that does not match the release

first_ten_seconds: Run it with --help: do you know what it does and how to start?
Run it with no arguments: does it do something safe and say what to do next?
Run it with a wrong flag: is the message short, clear and helpful?

checks.claim: --help shows a synopsis, every flag with what it does, and at least one example; --version prints the real version.
checks.how_to_inspect: Run the tool with --help and with --version and read both outputs as a newcomer.
checks.evidence_required: The --help and --version output exactly as printed.

checks.claim: Wrong or missing input gives a one-line explanation and the usage, with a non-zero exit, never a stack trace.
checks.how_to_inspect: Run it with an unknown flag, a missing argument and a file that does not exist.
checks.evidence_required: The three outputs and their exit codes.

source.quote: unknown flags fail cleanly with usage

checks.claim: It installs and runs from a clean environment (new folder, another user, a path with spaces), not only on the author's machine.
checks.how_to_inspect: Install into a fresh temporary folder whose path contains a space and run the documented first command.

source.section: 3. "Would this person look at this?" examples

checks.claim: A bare run changes nothing; destructive actions need an explicit flag or confirmation and offer a dry run.
checks.how_to_inspect: Run the tool with no flags in a scratch folder and compare the folder before and after; run each destructive command with --dry-run.
checks.evidence_required: The before and after listing and the dry-run output.

checks.claim: It was run on every operating system it claims to support (Windows and a POSIX shell at least, when both are claimed); untested platforms are labelled as such.
checks.how_to_inspect: Run the main commands on each claimed platform, or label the platforms where that did not happen.
checks.evidence_required: One transcript per platform, or the label in the docs.

source.quote: never claim "cross-platform" for an OS you did not actually run on

checks.claim: Normal output is written for the person reading it: short status lines in plain words, no internal ids or debugging noise.
checks.how_to_inspect: Run the main command and read every line as a beginner would; mark anything they would not understand.

source.section: 2. Sloppy / quality complaints, by deliverable type
source.quote: Status text written for the system, not for a beginner owner.

checks.claim: Exit 0 means success only; distinct failures get distinct non-zero codes, documented in --help or the docs.
checks.how_to_inspect: Trigger each failure class (usage, not found, runtime) and read the exit code of each.
checks.evidence_required: The exit code per failure class.

checks.claim: Data goes to stdout and logs, prompts and progress go to stderr, so a pipe stays clean.
checks.how_to_inspect: Run the tool with 2>/dev/null (or 2>$null) and check the remaining output is only data; pipe it into a parser.
checks.evidence_required: The piped run and its parsed result.

source.quote: Machine output → stdout; diagnostics, logs, prompts, progress → stderr

checks.claim: It never waits for input when stdin is not a terminal, and long work shows progress on stderr.
checks.how_to_inspect: Run it with stdin closed or redirected from an empty file and check that it finishes or fails with a message.
checks.evidence_required: The run with closed stdin and its exit code.

source.rationale: A prompt that waits forever in CI is a silent hang, found only when the pipeline times out.

checks.claim: Ctrl-C stops it cleanly: no half-written files, no orphan child processes.
checks.how_to_inspect: Start a long operation, press Ctrl-C, then check for partial files and leftover processes.
checks.evidence_required: The folder listing and process check after the interrupt.

checks.claim: Tests cover exit codes, stdout, stderr and piping, not only the core functions.
checks.how_to_inspect: Read the test file for assertions on exit code, stdout and stderr, and run it.
checks.evidence_required: The test run and the assertions found.

source.quote: Tests cover exit codes + stdout + stderr + pipe

checks.claim: A release users can see exists (a published package or release page, not only a tag), and its version matches --version.
checks.how_to_inspect: Open the package registry or release page and compare its version with the tool's --version output.
checks.evidence_required: The release URL or registry entry and the --version output (N/A when nothing is released).

source.section: 2. Sloppy / quality complaints, by deliverable type
source.quote: a release is not done until the GitHub Release exists

common_sloppy_defects.symptom: a mistyped flag prints 40 lines of internals instead of one line of usage
the CI step stays green although the tool printed an error
'Loading...' at the top of the JSON output breaks the parser
fails on Windows or in a folder whose path has a space
--help lists -f, -x, -q with no description and no example
